entry.title: Re: FM GUI_DOWNLOAD dump RAISE_EXCEPTION - NOT_SUPPORTED_BY_GUI
entry.content:
If the function module GUI_DOWNLOAD is called with the importing parameter CONFIRM_OVERWRITE or APPEND set to 'X' (it's called also via CL_GUI_FRONTEND_SERVICES=>GUI_DOWNLOAD), the method CL_GUI_FRONTEND_SERVICES=>FILE_EXIST is called by the function module without handling its exceptions so there's a short dump. Here's the culprit code in the function module GUI_DOWNLOAD:

IF NOT CONFIRM_OVERWRITE IS INITIAL OR NOT APPEND IS INITIAL.
  PRC_RESULT = CL_GUI_FRONTEND_SERVICES=>FILE_EXIST( FILENAME ).

The solution is:

  • either to fix the standard code inside the function module GUI_DOWNLOAD by handling the possible exceptions raised by FILE_EXIST (including NOT_SUPPORTED_BY_GUI),
  • or to change the custom program to not call GUI_DOWNLOAD (FM or method) if GUI is not supported by calling the method CL_GUI_FRONTEND_SERVICES=>CHECK_GUI_SUPPORT (that will detect any non-dialog process like a background job, etc.)

Sandra

NB: the bug exists at least in ABAP 7.58 SP 1 and I didn't find any SAP Note about it.

entry.title: Re: How are bank sub-accounts (clearing accounts) cleared?
entry.content:
Hi,

In this setup, the bank reconciliation account holds the confirmed bank balance, and the bank subaccount is the clearing account for payments in transfer. The subaccount is managed on an open item basis, and how it is cleared depends on which document comes first.

1. Outgoing payments (payment first, bank statement later)
- Payment entry (payment run or outgoing payment): Dr Vendor / Cr Bank subaccount. This clears the vendor and creates an open item on the subaccount.
- Bank statement: Dr Bank subaccount / Cr Bank reconciliation account. This clears the subaccount.

2. Incoming receipts (bank statement first, receipt later)
- Bank statement: Dr Bank reconciliation account / Cr Bank subaccount, when the customer cannot be identified automatically.
- Receipt posting (bank statement post-processing): Dr Bank subaccount / Cr Customer. This clears the subaccount and the customer.

Clearing methods
1. Electronic bank statement with interpretation algorithms (main method): the system uses the reference returned by the bank to find and clear the open item, for example 020 (document number search), 021 (reference number search), 019 (DME reference) or 011/012/013 for checks.
2. Bank statement reprocessing: statement items that could not be matched are cleared manually by selecting the open item.
3. Automatic G/L clearing job: remaining items are cleared using clearing criteria such as Assignment or Reference with a zero balance.
4. Manual G/L clearing: for any items still open.

 

Hope this helps.

entry.title: Implementing Dynamic Approvals in SAP SmartRecruiter
entry.content:
The Problem: Static Approval Chains

By default, SmartRecruiter allows you to configure Sequential or Parallel approval chains where the list of approvers is fixed at configuration time. This works well for homogeneous workflows, but breaks down when business rules require different approvers based on runtime data.

Two scenarios that call for dynamic routing:

  • Job approval: If the total compensation package is >= 100 (e.g., LPA), it must be approved by User A and User B; otherwise, by User A and User C.
  • Offer approval: If the salary hike is <= 50%, approvers are A and B; if 50–100%, approvers are A, B, and C; if > 100%, approvers are A, B, and the Head of Department.

These rules cannot be pre-configured statically. The solution is an Integration-type approval chain that delegates control to an external CPI flow at runtime.

Setting Up an Integration-Type Approval Chain in SmartRecruiter

Navigate to Settings > Job Approvals in SmartRecruiter and create a new approval chain. Instead of selecting Sequential or Parallel, choose the Integration tab. This tells SmartRecruiter that an external integration (your CPI iFlow) is responsible for managing the approval process.

Inside the chain configuration, set the Approval Chain type to Integration and select your registered CPI application as the App Integration. All scope fields can be set to 'All selected' for a global rule or scoped down as needed.

Key concept: When an Integration-type chain is active, SmartRecruiter assigns a system/integration user as the initial placeholder approver. This user acts as a signal to your CPI flow that the approval needs to be re-assigned dynamically.

What Happens When a Job Is Created

Once the integration chain is active, creating a new job in SmartRecruiter will automatically route the approval to the configured integration user (system user). The job moves into a 'Pending approval' state.

The webhook event job.approval.created fires at this point, triggering your CPI iFlow to take over the approval routing.

Implementing Dynamic Approval Logic in CPI

Your CPI iFlow receives the job.approval.created webhook payload. A Groovy script within the flow reads the relevant job or offer fields, evaluates the business rules, and determines the correct approvers. The implementation follows two API calls to SmartRecruiter.

Step 1: Get the Current Approval (Retrieve baseId)

Call the following endpoint to retrieve the latest approval for the job:

GET https://api.smartrecruiters.com/jobs/{jobId}/approvals/latest

The response includes the approvalRequestId which becomes the baseId for the next call.

Step 2: Create a New Approval with Dynamic Approvers

POST to the Approvals API with the baseId and the dynamically determined approver list:

POST https://api.smartrecruiters.com/approvals-api/v201910/approvals

Request Body:

{
  "baseId": "35a1ef73-4542-4d37-84c2-2b34522327e1",
  "type": "sequential",
  "decisionMode": "any",
  "steps": [
    {
      "approvers": [
        { "id": "6a986436be2958fa852dda78" }   // User A
      ]
    },
    {
      "approvers": [
        { "id": "6a98643697a14f8c43c2a454" }   // User B or C (from Groovy logic)
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Verifying the Dynamic Approval on the SmartRecruiter UI

After the CPI iFlow completes the POST call, refresh the job in SmartRecruiter. The approval panel will now show the dynamically assigned approvers — replacing the original integration user with the correct business approvers as determined by the Groovy logic.

Triggering the Integration via Webhook

The entire flow is event-driven. Configure a SmartRecruiter webhook to fire your CPI iFlow endpoint whenever a job or offer approval is created.

Extending to Offer Approvals

The exact same pattern applies to offer approvals. The only differences are:

  • GET endpoint to fetch the baseId:
    https://api.smartrecruiters.com/candidates/{id}/jobs/{jobId}/offers/{offerId}/approvals/latest
  • Webhook event: offer.approval.created (instead of job.approval.created).
  • The POST endpoint and request body structure remain identical.

Tip: Reuse the same CPI iFlow for both job and offer approvals by routing on the webhook event type at the message entry point. A single Groovy script can contain all business-rule branches, keyed on the approval subject type ('job' vs 'offer') in the GET response.

Conclusion

The Integration-type approval chain in SAP SmartRecruiter, combined with the Approvals API and SAP CPI, provides a clean, scalable pattern for implementing dynamic, condition-driven approval workflows. Instead of creating dozens of static chains to cover every business scenario, you centralise the routing logic in a single CPI iFlow and let the API handle the assignment at runtime.

This approach is equally applicable to re-triggering rejected approvals — simply listen for the approval-rejected webhook, run your re-routing logic, and POST a fresh approval using the same baseId.

I hope this blog gives you a clear blueprint to get started. Feel free to share your questions or experiences in the comments below!

Thanks

Kunal

entry.title: Free Joule Studio certification (C_JSD): how to claim it and plan the 24 hours (EN/PT)
entry.content:
Versão em português mais abaixo.

English version

Hi everyone,

A certification exam where you don't pick A, B or C. You build an AI agent and then show it to an AI avatar that asks you questions about what you built. And this time the attempt is free.

That is the new SAP Certified - Joule Studio Developer, exam code C_JSD. SAP Learning published the official announcement here in the Community today (link at the end), and the offer is also on the SAP TechEd page of SAP Learning. I shared a short version of this on LinkedIn. This is the full one, with every detail checked on SAP's own pages today, October 27, 2026.

What you get

  • One free attempt per person, valid through December 31, 2026. You can sign up only once.
  • No SAP Learning Hub subscription, no certification purchase, no BTP subaccount and no Joule Studio subscription. SAP gives you a pre-configured Joule Studio practice system.
  • Open to anyone with an SAP Universal ID. The FAQ says there is no restriction based on company type, role or geography.

How the exam works

It is performance-based. First you complete the hands-on exercises in the practice system, and that part is mandatory. Then comes the scenario-based assessment: an AI roleplay where an avatar asks you to show the agents you built and answer questions about them.

  • The certification page lists 2 hours and a 60% pass score.
  • AI roleplay languages: English, Spanish, Italian, French and Japanese. No Portuguese, which matters for us in Brazil.
  • There is a non-AI alternative: you record a video answering the open questions. English only, reviewed by people, and the result can take up to 20 business days. With the AI roleplay the result usually comes right after you submit, or shortly after.
  • What it validates, according to SAP: turning a business idea into a deployable agent (intent-based development), building and extending agents, grounding them in SAP business context, and managing deployment and lifecycle.

The detail that matters most: the 24 hours

From the FAQ: "After enrolling to the practice system, you have 24h to complete the tasks and the exam." The exercises and the exam have to fit in the same 24 hours.

So the clock does not start when you claim the voucher. It starts when you enter the practice system. My advice: claim it now, study first, and only open the practice system on a day you can really dedicate to it.

Step by step

  1. Check your SAP Universal ID (you can create one for free at account.sap.com). The FAQ asks for two different email accounts assigned to it. Fix that before you start.
  2. Open the campaign page (link at the end), log in with your SAP Universal ID and accept the Terms and Conditions. The attempt is assigned to your account.
  3. Study the learning journey (next section). Don't open the practice system yet.
  4. Go through the Technical Readiness Checklist (browser, connection), linked on the certification page.
  5. On your free day: enroll in the practice system and finish all the exercises.
  6. Still inside the 24 hours: go to the certification page, find the Joule Studio certification and click "Start exam". No scheduling needed.
  7. If you pass, the badge and the certificate show up in the Certification section of your SAP Learning profile.

What to study

  • The learning journey "Developing with Joule Studio": what Joule Studio is and where it sits in the SAP Business AI Platform, then creating agents, extending existing agents and building n8n workflows inside Joule Studio. The FAQ says completing it is "strongly recommended".
  • The journey lists "Understanding AI" as a prerequisite. If AI agents are new to you, start there.
  • The scenario-based assessment FAQ, so you know what the AI roleplay looks like before you face it.

If it doesn't work out

It is a real exam, with one attempt. A failed campaign attempt does not count against your commercial attempt limits, but you cannot sign up for the campaign again. After it ends, you can buy an attempt or use the ones you already have, from January 1, 2027.

If SAP changes any rule, the FAQ wins over this post. If you already took it, tell me in the comments how your 24 hours went. I'm curious about the roleplay part.

Versão em português

Oi, pessoal,

Uma prova de certificação em que você não marca A, B ou C. Você constrói um agente de IA e depois mostra ele para um avatar de IA que faz perguntas sobre o que você construiu. E desta vez a tentativa é gratuita.

É a nova SAP Certified - Joule Studio Developer, código C_JSD. A SAP Learning publicou hoje o anúncio oficial aqui na Community (link no fim), e a oferta também está na página do SAP TechEd no SAP Learning. Postei uma versão curta no LinkedIn. Esta é a completa, com cada detalhe conferido hoje, 27/10/2026, nas páginas da própria SAP.

O que você ganha

  • Uma tentativa gratuita por pessoa, válida até 31/12/2026. Só dá para se inscrever uma vez.
  • Não precisa de assinatura do SAP Learning Hub, nem comprar prova, nem subconta de BTP, nem assinatura do Joule Studio. A SAP entrega um ambiente de prática do Joule Studio já configurado.
  • Aberta a qualquer pessoa com SAP Universal ID. A FAQ diz que não há restrição por tipo de empresa, função ou país.

Como é a prova

É prática. Primeiro você faz os exercícios no ambiente de prática, e essa parte é obrigatória. Depois vem a avaliação por cenário: um roleplay com IA em que um avatar pede para você mostrar os agentes que construiu e responder perguntas sobre eles.

  • A página da certificação informa 2 horas e nota de aprovação de 60%.
  • Idiomas do roleplay com IA: inglês, espanhol, italiano, francês e japonês. Português não está na lista, então para nós fica inglês ou espanhol.
  • Existe a alternativa sem IA: você grava um vídeo respondendo às perguntas abertas. Só em inglês, avaliado por pessoas, e o resultado pode levar até 20 dias úteis. No roleplay com IA o resultado costuma sair logo depois do envio, ou pouco depois.
  • O que ela valida, segundo a SAP: transformar uma ideia de negócio num agente pronto para implantar (desenvolvimento por intenção), criar e estender agentes, ancorar esses agentes no contexto de negócio SAP e cuidar da implantação e do ciclo de vida.

O detalhe que mais importa: as 24 horas

Da FAQ: "After enrolling to the practice system, you have 24h to complete the tasks and the exam." Os exercícios e a prova têm de caber nas mesmas 24 horas.

Ou seja, o relógio não começa quando você pega o voucher. Ele começa quando você entra no ambiente de prática. Meu conselho: garanta a vaga agora, estude antes e só abra o ambiente num dia em que você consiga se dedicar de verdade.

Passo a passo

  1. Confira o seu SAP Universal ID (dá para criar de graça em account.sap.com). A FAQ pede dois e-mails diferentes cadastrados nele. Acerte isso antes de começar.
  2. Abra a página da campanha (link no fim), entre com o SAP Universal ID e aceite os Termos e Condições. A tentativa fica atribuída à sua conta.

  5. No dia livre: entre no ambiente de prática e termine todos os exercícios.

  7. Aprovado, o badge e o certificado aparecem na seção Certification do seu perfil no SAP Learning.

O que estudar

  • A trilha "Developing with Joule Studio": o que é o Joule Studio e onde ele fica na SAP Business AI Platform, depois criar agentes, estender agentes existentes e montar workflows de n8n dentro do Joule Studio. A FAQ diz que concluir a trilha é "strongly recommended".

Se não der certo

É prova de verdade, com uma tentativa. Reprovação na tentativa da campanha não conta no seu limite de tentativas pagas, mas não dá para se inscrever na campanha de novo. Depois que ela acabar, você pode comprar uma tentativa ou usar as que já tem, a partir de 01/01/2027.

entry.title: What I Learned Moving an Acquired Workforce (M&A) from Workday to SuccessFactors: 11 Lessons
entry.content:
What I Learned Moving an Acquired Workforce from Workday to SuccessFactors: 11 Lessons

What to plan for when moving an acquired company's employees onto a new HR system

Moving an acquired company's employees to a new HR system sounds simple: copy the data and hit a deadline. In practice, the system is often the easy part. The hard parts are outside vendors, agreements with acquired company, other projects going live at the same time, and things people assumed but never checked.

This lists eleven areas to plan for. They come from my experience moving an acquired workforce from Workday to SAP SuccessFactors.

At a glance

#

Area

What can go wrong

What to do?

1

Different vendors

The acquired company uses other payroll, time, and benefits providers.

Identify and decide who moves to the parent's vendors and who stays. If parent company selects new vendors let's say for time tracking for some countries then do plan in advance and align with the vendors.

2

Acquired Company agreement (TSA - Transition Services Agreement )

The acquired company may still run some services, so acquired company employees must not go to new vendors yet but will use existing services from legacy vendor.

In Integrations, add a filter by employee group and test it to ensure right employee population flows to the vendors.

3

Logins ready early

If accounts are made after the production employee data load,  the conveyed employees (acquired company employees) cannot get in on day one.

Usually accounts are activated and business email is created when employees are added to the system. In M&A projects, IT should plan this ahead in time so conveyed employees are able to login on day one.

4

Software updates

The software vendor updates, e.g. SuccessFactors - twice a year can change what you tested.

Updates should be reviewed and tested on priority

5

Parent Company Other Projects

The parent company may switch other tools on the go-live date or may have other internal HCM projects planned.

List the overlaps. Agree what comes first. Create a critical path based upon priorities.

6

Business keeps moving

Hires and changes continue during the move.

Set a freeze period for all HCM processes in parent and acquired company systems

7

Year-end timing

If it's a January go-live, it usually clashes with payroll year-end and holidays.

Check who is available. Plan extra support over the holidays.

8

Languages

The parent's system and documents may lack the acquired company's languages.

Check language support early. Translate legal items first. Plan job aid translations and system translations accordingly.

9

Training

Training is the first thing cut when time is short.

Train managers first. Keep it short and by role.

10

New countries and policies

The parent may never have set up some of the countries.

Use a checklist for each country, work with Legal and plan to keep it simple as critical path for go-live.

11

Approvals and alignment with legal and works council

Legal approvals and work council approvals are critical

Treat approvals as must-haves.

 

PART 1

Vendors and connections

1   Different vendors

In short: The acquired company rarely uses the same vendors as the parent.

  • Payroll. This is the most sensitive area. Decide early whether employees move to the parent's payroll provider on day one, stay with their current one, or move country by country. Staying is often safest for the first pay runs, but it means building and testing an extra connection.
  • Time tracking. Hours worked drive pay. If shift rules or extra pay rates do not match, pay will be wrong.
  • Vendor availability. Each extra vendor is a team you do not control hence plan properly.
  • Vendor setup. Security checks and access approvals can take longer than the build itself.

2   The acquired company agreement decides who goes where

In short: A Transition Services Agreement (TSA) means the acquired company keeps providing some services, such as payroll or benefits, for a set time.

  • Use a filter. A simple rule, such as a flag, decides which employees are sent to which vendor, and when that changes.
  • Test both ways. Add the filter to every connection. Check who is sent and who is not.
  • Plan the end. When the TSA ends, the filter is removed. Treat that as its own go-live.

Without this, someone may be paid twice, not paid at all, or sent to a vendor they should not be in.

3   Logins must be ready before go-live

In short: People cannot log in if their accounts do not exist yet.

  • Create accounts early. If access depends on the company's login system, such as Active Directory or single sign-on, accounts may not exist when the data arrives. Create them before the data load.
  • Know the login method. Whether people sign in with the company login or a password decides who fixes lockouts and resets.
  • Test as a real employee. Try the first login the way an employee would, not as an administrator.
  • Agree on names. Settle usernames, email formats, number ranges for objects and employees, and whether employee IDs stay the same.

PART 2

Timing and change

4   Software updates follow their own calendar

In short: Updates can change features you already tested.

Cloud software like SuccessFactors gets major updates twice a year, and the dates will not match your project plan. On this project, an update affected the performance module for which the fix from SAP was planned on date which was late for the project so feature was disabled and we had to go with an old version of the performance template.

  • Put update dates on the project calendar from the start.
  • Re-test what already worked after each update.
  • Give one person the job of reading the release notes.

5   Other projects at the parent go live too

In short: Your go-live date is rarely the only change.

The parent company may switch other tools on the same date, for example moving the employee help desk from Employee Central Service Center to ServiceNow, or changing a payroll provider.

  • List the overlaps. Find where the other projects touch yours, such as ticket types, workflows, connections, and links employees use.
  • Decide what comes first. If one change slips, agree which has priority and who decides.
  • Prepare support. Make sure acquired employees know where to send requests on day one, with help articles and trained agents.
  • Share one calendar. Everyone should see freeze periods, test dates, and announcements from other projects.
  • Watch shared people. The same experts, testers, and approvers are often needed by both projects.

6   The business does not stop during the move

In short: Hires, exits, promotions, and team changes keep happening.

  • Set a freeze. Stop changes in the old system for a short time, and decide how to handle changes made during it.
  • Plan a final load. Catch changes made after the last data copy.
  • Watch recent changes. Promotions, transfers, and pay changes with dates close to go-live are easy to miss.
  • Name an owner. Decide who enters anything that falls through by hand.

7   Go-live often lands on year-end

In short: A January 1 go-live collides with payroll year-end, tax reports, and holidays.

  • Check people's availability over the go-live weekend and the days after.
  • Check vendor freezes. Many vendors stop changes around year-end.
  • Plan extra support around holiday cover, not the usual work calendar.

PART 3

People and experience

8   Languages: the acquired company may have more than the parent

In short: The parent's system and documents may not cover every language the acquired company uses.

  • Check language support in screens, forms, and notices for every country. Gaps tend to show up late.
  • Translate the important items first: privacy notices, offer letters, policies, and how-to guides.
  • Have a native speaker review translations, especially legal wording.
  • Remember works councils often ask for translated materials before they can review.

9   Training gets squeezed

In short: Training is usually the first thing cut, yet employees and managers must work in the new system.

  • Train managers first. They answer most questions and run processes like performance and onboarding.
  • Keep it short. Quick guides, short videos, and live walk-throughs beat long courses.
  • Time it well. Training too early is forgotten, and too late does not help.
  • Cover all time zones and languages, and record sessions for people who cannot attend.
  • Offer extra support after go-live. Daily open sessions in the first weeks catch what training missed.

10   New countries, policies, and default settings

In short: The acquired company may have employees in countries the parent has never set up.

  • New country setup needs local fields, templates, and legal checks.
  • Policy gaps are common, such as a time-off policy for a country where the parent has none. That can mean tracking by hand or buying a tool.
  • Default settings can quietly cause errors, such as working hours for new hires or end-of-employment steps.
  • Systems do not match one-to-one. Understand the idea first, then match the fields.

 

PART 4

Control and quality

11   Legal approvals and data loads can move the date

In short: Some of the most important items are not technical.

  • Works councils. In countries such as Germany, an employee representative body may need to be informed, consulted, or give approval before employee data moves. Treat approval as a must-have for go-live.
  • Offer letters and contract templates. They need legal review for the new employer and local law. If the hiring tool's build waits on that review, so does its testing.
  • Data loading side effects. Changes to drop-down lists need a plan for existing records. Mass changes can trigger messages and files to other systems. Check the numbers after every test load.

entry.title: SAP TechEd 2026 — Day 1: O Resumo que Você Precisa Ler
entry.content:
O que aconteceu hoje em Berlim?

O SAP TechEd 2026 começou hoje em Berlim e o primeiro dia já veio carregado. O evento vai até quarta-feira (29/10) e pode ser acompanhado de graça na versão virtual. Aqui vai o resumo do Day 1 para quem quer ficar por dentro sem precisar assistir tudo.

Mão na massa desde o primeiro minuto

O Developer Garage abriu as portas logo cedo — é o espaço onde você senta, abre o laptop e experimenta as novidades com zero pressão. Tutoriais prontos, ferramentas carregadas e o time da SAP ali do lado para ajudar. Não é palestra: é prática.

Um "guardião" para toda a IA da empresa

Uma das maiores novidades do dia foi o SAP Enterprise AI Gateway. Pense nele como um painel de controle central para tudo que envolve IA dentro da empresa: quem acessa o quê, quais modelos estão sendo usados, quanto está sendo consumido e se tudo está dentro das regras.

Isso importa porque, à medida que empresas adotam vários agentes e modelos de IA ao mesmo tempo, o risco de perder o controle cresce. O gateway resolve isso com uma camada única de segurança, monitoramento e auditoria.

Ele funciona com protocolos abertos (MCP e A2A), o que significa que agentes de diferentes fornecedores podem trabalhar juntos sem que a empresa perca a governança. Está planejado para o primeiro trimestre de 2027.

A IA da SAP agora faz, não só sugere

A keynote trouxe uma frase que resume tudo: a SAP está passando de uma IA que aprende o negócio para uma IA que opera o negócio.

O Joule Work é o exemplo mais concreto disso. Você descreve um objetivo — tipo "preciso aprovar estas ordens de compra" — e agentes de IA planejam os passos e executam tudo no seu landscape SAP, de ponta a ponta.

Outro destaque foi o SAP-RPT-2.0, o modelo de IA para dados estruturados. Ele agora detecta anomalias automaticamente (ex.: um pagamento fora do padrão) e faz previsões de negócio sem exigir que você monte um projeto de machine learning do zero. E a parte mais impressionante: esse modelo foi levado para a Estação Espacial Internacional em parceria com a HPE, onde roda diretamente a bordo para prever falhas em equipamentos sem precisar enviar dados de volta à Terra.

Além disso, a SAP está oferecendo a certificação Joule Studio Developer de graça até 31 de dezembro de 2026 — uma boa oportunidade para quem quer se preparar para essa nova era.

ABAP está mais vivo do que nunca

Para quem trabalha ou está começando com ABAP, o recado do Day 1 foi forte: o ABAP não vai embora — ele está evoluindo com IA.

Agora existe um ABAP MCP Server que permite que qualquer ferramenta de IA interaja diretamente com sistemas ABAP. O desenvolvimento em VS Code está ganhando suporte cada vez maior. E o SAP-ABAP-1, um modelo de IA treinado especificamente no código ABAP da SAP, já está disponível para ajudar a escrever código, gerar testes e acelerar migrações.

Traduzindo: se você é developer ABAP, as ferramentas que vão turbinar seu dia a dia estão chegando — e muitas já estão disponíveis.

Amanhã tem mais — e você pode participar de graça

O Day 1 foi só o começo. Amanhã (28/10) o evento continua com sessões técnicas, workshops hands-on e mais anúncios — incluindo a noite de celebração dos 30 anos do SAP TechEd.

O melhor: a versão virtual é gratuita. Você se registra, acompanha as keynotes ao vivo e acessa o conteúdo on demand depois. Não precisa estar em Berlim para aproveitar.

entry.title: SAP Managed Integration for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition -- adoption experience
entry.content:
SAP Managed Integration for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition

From an integration project to an adoption experience

Already running SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition and ready to adopt another SAP solution? SAP-Managed Integration simplifies the connection by letting SAP handle the supported technical integration—helping you get started with less effort.

This post kicks off a multipart blog series. We'll introduce SAP-Managed Integration and its value for customers, then explore individual integration scenarios in the posts that follow.

When a customer wants to adopt another SAP solution with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, the business case is clear. The products are ready. Then the integration work begins: connectivity, trust, technical users, certificates, integration content and coordination across teams.

The customer wanted a business capability. Getting there also meant assembling and maintaining the technical connection.

SAP-Managed Integration simplifies this work for supported SAP-to-SAP scenarios. Customers request activation, fulfill the prerequisites and carry out business testing. SAP handles the technical integration and manages it throughout its lifecycle.

Why lifecycle ownership matters

Integration effort continues after go-live. Credentials change, certificates expire, software evolves and connectivity needs monitoring. Each new connection can add another operational responsibility to the customer landscape.

SAP-Managed Integration is a product model in which SAP operates supported technical integration components. Automation helps establish the connection; managed ownership helps keep it working.

This builds on SAP's work to simplify integration setup. SAP Help guidance for connecting SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition with supported SAP product provides the scenario-specific setup context. The managed model extends the focus from executing configuration steps to owning supported technical lifecycle activities.

The customer journey

The experience starts with intent: the customer wants to use another supported SAP solution with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition. The customer then enables the required entitlements and access and prepares customer-controlled infrastructure where the scenario requires it.

Once prerequisites are fulfilled, the customer activates the supported integration. SAP performs the managed technical configuration, while the customer focuses on business testing and adoption.

The six stages below outline the customer journey. The exact activities vary by integration scenario and landscape readiness.

What SAP manages and what customers control

SAP manages the supported technical integration components: the relevant integration lifecycle, SAP namespace artifacts, supported connectivity and trust configuration, technical credential management, monitoring and maintenance.

Customers retain control of entitlements, customer-managed infrastructure, user authorizations control, data scope and business validation. SAP Cloud Connector installation and infrastructure remain customer responsibilities where required. Customers also initiate their SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition upgrades; SAP manages the supported integration lifecycle activities associated with those changes.

This responsibility model gives customer teams a clearer operating boundary. Business decisions remain with the customer, and supported integration operations move into SAP's managed service scope.

The value continues after activation

  • Faster time to value. Reducing technical setup and coordination helps teams reach business validation sooner.
  • Lower customer effort. IT teams can spend more time on processes, data and adoption, with less routine work on supported SAP-to-SAP integration components.
  • Clearer operational accountability. Monitoring and maintenance of managed components have an identified owner across the integration lifecycle.
  • Better lifecycle continuity. Supported integration changes are managed as part of the service as SAP components evolve.
  • A more connected suite experience. A consistent activation and operating model makes it easier to adopt additional supported SAP capabilities.

Starting with data and AI and expanding across the SAP suite

Our roadmap brings SAP-Managed Integration to customers in successive waves, simplifying the adoption of more SAP capabilities along the way.

Connecting your data — SAP-Managed Business Data Cloud integration

Currently in beta testing, this integration simplifies the connection between SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition and SAP Business Data Cloud, helping customers make ERP data available for analytics and intelligent applications with less technical effort.

Enabling your AI experience — SAP-Managed Joule integration

Currently in Early Adopter Care, SAP-Managed Joule integration brings the managed experience to AI. By simplifying secure connections to business applications, context and processes, it helps customers focus on adopting Joule and agent capabilities.

Bringing more of your SAP landscape together — The road ahead

The roadmap extends to additional SAP solutions, including SAP SuccessFactors and next-generation SAP Ariba. Each expansion advances the same ambition: make connecting supported SAP solutions an activation experience, with SAP managing the technical integration lifecycle.

Availability and prerequisites vary by scenario. Roadmap scope and timelines are subject to change.

Getting started

  1. Identify the supported SAP solution you want to connect with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition. Review its prerequisites, release requirements and responsibility model.
  2. Initiate the applicable enablement process through SAP for Me.
  3. Prepare customer-controlled access and infrastructure, then activate the supported scenario.
  4. Validate the business outcome. SAP then manages the technical components within the agreed service scope.

You choose what you want to connect. SAP manages the supported integration.

Which part of your integration journey consumes the most effort today: setup, cross-team coordination or ongoing maintenance? Share your experience in the comments.

Capabilities and supported scenarios vary by solution, release and customer landscape. The applicable documentation and service description define prerequisites, commercial terms, scope and responsibilities.

entry.title: Personnel Calculation Rule - OUTWP
entry.content:
Introduction:

In SAP HCM, payroll processing is rarely a one-size-fits-all model; logic often varies dynamically based on an employee’s role, department, location, and working hours. To accommodate these diverse business requirements, consultants rely heavily on Personnel Calculation Rules (PCRs) and Functions within the payroll schema. In this blog post, we will explore a practical, step-by-step approach to creating a multi-level conditional PCR that evaluates an employee's Personnel Area, Personnel Subarea, and Work Schedule before driving specific wage type calculations.

 PCR Case:

Payroll plays a major role in each and every employee who works in a company. But those Calculations vary company to company, employee role, department, location, work time and various other factors. All these calculations can be achieved in Payroll PCRs and Functions which will be assigned in a schema.

Lets take a condition where we have to fetch Personnel area, Personnel Subarea and Work schedule and calculation should differ based on certain personnel area, personnel subarea and Work Schedule.

Logic:

*
****
OUTWPPLANT
1037
GCY Z**1A

A
****
OUTWPPLTSC
U**3
GCY Z**1B

B
****
OUTWPSHIFT
XXXX_XX
GCY Z**1C

Calculation happens based on the mentioned formula.

Personal Experience:

when I got multiple level of condition to check before performing a calculation, I had two options either to go with payroll functions or PCR. In PCR OUTWP plays a major role for fetching or checking multiple parameters such as Payroll area, Personnel area, Personnel Subarea, Work schedule, Country modifier, Employee Group, Employee Sub-group, Pay scale type, etc. By using this function you can achieve these condition in PCR level instead of choosing Payroll function. The below PCR explanation help you understand how I achieved my case in PCR.

PCR Image:

PCR Line by line Explanation:

Initially this PCR checks for Wage Type. “****” allows all wage types.

If Personnel Area = 1037

Then:

Calls PCR ZTS1A(nothing but the A condition in same PCR)

Inside A:

Checks IF personnel Subarea = UK03

Then:

Calls PCR ZTS1B(Similar to previous step)

Inside B:

Checks IF Work schedule = GPWS_WSR

Then:

Calls ZTS1C( Where Calculation happens)

Summary:

Here we check personnel area, personnel subarea and work schedule step by step in 3 level of condition and then performs calculation for a particular wage type and store the values.

Conclusion:

By structuring conditional logic using operations like OUTWPPLANT, OUTWPPLTSC, and OUTWPSHIFT, you can build precise, multi-tiered PCRs that handle complex organizational dependencies seamlessly within SAP Payroll. This granular approach ensures that calculations are tailored exactly to specific business units and schedules while maintaining clean, maintainable schema structures. entry.title: Identity Propagation from Joule to SAP SuccessFactors
entry.content:
During workforce management reviews, HR managers and administrators frequently need to audit employee contract extension data. Searching through nested SAP SuccessFactors menus or manually parsing custom Metadata Framework (MDF) objects introduces friction into routine operations.

By integrating Joule with custom extension agents on SAP BTP, users can query sensitive custom MDF objects—such as Contract Renewal entities—using natural language while dynamically enforcing SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP) for every tool call.

Scenario Overview

  • Intent Initiation via Digital Assistant: An HR administrator or standard employee queries Joule using natural language to retrieve or verify contract renewal cases for an employee.
  • Identity Propagation & Session Context: Joule interprets the prompt and executes user identity propagation (principal propagation) down to SAP SuccessFactors, ensuring that the authenticated user's session context is preserved end-to-end.
  • Context-Aware RBP Enforcement: The custom agent fetches data directly from SuccessFactors OData APIs. Access to sensitive fields (such as salary adjustments or contract terms) is governed entirely by the user's assigned SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions.

This article walks through the end-to-end configuration: setting up trust between Joule and SuccessFactors, enabling principal propagation, and enforcing role-based access to the custom Contract Renewal MDF object.

Prerequisites

To successfully implement this architecture, ensure that the following system dependencies and administrative privileges are in place:

  • SAP BTP Subaccount with Joule Enabled: An active subaccount on SAP BTP with the Joule digital assistant entitlement subscribed and provisioned.
  • SAP Identity Authentication Service (IAS): An IAS tenant configured as the Identity Provider for both your SAP BTP subaccount and your SAP SuccessFactors instance to enable OpenID Connect (OIDC) and SAML token exchanges.
  • Custom MDF Object in SuccessFactors: A custom Metadata Framework (MDF) object—such as Contract Renewal—created via Configure Object Definitions in SuccessFactors.
  • Role-Based Permissions (RBP) Configured: Specific permissions assigned in SuccessFactors RBP for the custom MDF object (e.g., read/write access granted to HR Manager, and restricted for Standard User).
  • Administrative Access: Administrator privileges across the SAP BTP Cockpit, the SAP IAS Administration Console, and the SuccessFactors Admin Center.
  • Protocol Familiarity: Basic understanding of OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect (OIDC), JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and SAML 2.0 bearer assertions.

Architecture Overview

The following diagram illustrates the end-to-end trust chain and identity flow between Joule, SAP BTP, SAP Cloud Identity Services, and SAP SuccessFactors:
 
The identity flow begins when a user authenticates in Joule via SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS). Joule’s A2A client routes the prompt through a BTP Destination to the pro-code custom agent on SAP Cloud Foundry. The agent validates and forwards the user token, using a second BTP Destination to execute a SAML Bearer Assertion against SAP SuccessFactors. This ensures the request hits the OData API Center with the user's active session context, dynamically enforcing Role-Based Permissions (RBP) at the backend metadata layer.
 

Generate the SAML Signing Certificate

The BTP Destination Service will sign SAML assertions using a certificate. SuccessFactors needs that certificate registered to trust those assertions. Two commands are needed here because the outputs serve two different purposes and go to two different systems.

The first command generates the raw key material in PEM format — certificate.pem  is the public certificate you upload to SuccessFactors, and privateKey.pem is the private key that stays on your machine.

openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 3650 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout certs/privateKey.pem \
  -out certs/certificate.pem \
  -subj "/CN=sfsf-assistant-saml"

The second command takes those two PEM files and bundles them together into a PKCS#12 keystore (.p12). This is the format BTP Destination Service expects when it needs to sign SAML assertions on behalf of your application — a plain PEM file is not sufficient for this purpose.

openssl pkcs12 -export \
  -in certs/certificate.pem \
  -inkey certs/privateKey.pem \
  -out certs/sfsf-saml-client.p12 \
  -name "sfsf-saml-client" \
  -password pass:yourpassword

certificate.pem goes to SuccessFactors when registering the OAuth2 client. sfsf-saml-client.p12 goes to the BTP Destination Service certificate store. Remember, the password for your .p12 certificate will be required when you use it in the destination configuration. 

Register an OAuth2 Client in SuccessFactors

SuccessFactors needs to know your app's signing certificate before it will accept SAML assertions from it.

1. Log in to SuccessFactors Admin Center. Navigate to Admin Center → Manage OAuth2 Client Applications or Under the tools Search field type Manage OAuth2 Client Applications and click the link in the search results.

2. Click Register Client Application

3. When you click Register Client Application under Manage OAuth2 Client Applications in SAP SuccessFactors, you will need to fill out the following form fields:

  • Company: Pre-filled automatically based on your current SuccessFactors instance or tenant ID.
  • Application Name: A unique, descriptive name for your client application or integration.
  • Description (Optional): A short note explaining the purpose of the application or integration.
  • Application URL: A valid URL pointing to the client application or vendor's website domain.
  • X.509 Certificate: Paste your pre-generated public certificate text which we generated in the previous section.

and click Register

4. After clicking Register, the system generates a public API Key required for authenticating your API requests. To retrieve this key, locate your new client entry in the list, navigate to the Actions column, and click View.

5.Locate the generated API Key. Copy it and store it safely, as your external application will require it to complete the connection.

Maintain the Generated Certificate in BTP Destination Service

Before configuring the destination itself, the .p12 keystore must be uploaded to the BTP Destination Service certificate store. The destination references it by name — it is never embedded inline.

1. Login into the SAP BTP Cockpit and navigate to your Subaccount. Go to Connectivity and navigate directly to Destination Certificates and click on Import Button.

2. Click the Upload button to select your certificate file from your local file system

3. Select sfsf-saml-client.p12  from your local machine and click on Open button.

4. Click on Create button

Once uploaded, the certificate appears in the list with the name sfsf-saml-client.p12. This is the exact value you will enter as Key Store Location when configuring the sfsf-conn destination.

The certificate store is scoped to your BTP subaccount. Multiple destinations in the same subaccount can reference the same uploaded keystore.

Import the Destinations

With the certificate uploaded, you can now create the destination that performs the actual principal propagation. This destination is what your application calls to exchange the user's IAS token for a SuccessFactors OAuth token.
Rather than filling in every property manually, download the pre-built destination file below and import it directly into BTP. You only need to update the four placeholder values specific to your SuccessFactors tenant before importing.

Download: (destinations/sfsf-conn.properties)

Open the file and replace the following placeholders with your own values:

Authentication=OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
KeyStoreLocation=sfsf-saml-client.p12
KeyStorePassword=<keystore-password>
Name=sfsf-conn
ProxyType=Internet
SAMLAssertionProvider=DestinationServiceGenerated
Type=HTTP
URL=<successfactors-api-url>
apiKey=<generated-api-key-in-successfactor>
audience=www.successfactors.com
authnContextClassRef=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PreviousSession
clientKey=<generated-api-key-in-successfactor>
companyId=<company-id-in-successfactor>
includeSigningCertificateInSAMLAssertion=true
nameIdFormat=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:unspecified
skipUserAttributesPrefixInSAMLAttributes=true
skipUserUuidInSAMLAttributes=true
tokenServiceURL=<successfactors-api-url>/oauth/token
tokenServiceURLType=Dedicated
  • <successfactors-api-url>:  SAP  API domain (e.g., api12sales.successfactors.eu) — appears in both URL and tokenServiceURL
  • <generated-api-key-in-successfactor>: The API Key (Client ID) generated during OAuth2 registration in SF — appears in both clientKey and apiKey.
  • <company-id-in-successfactor>:  Your SAP SF company/tenant ID.
  • <keystore-password>:  The password set for the uploaded .p12 X.509 certificate used for SAML signing.

All other properties — authentication type, SAML settings, certificate flags — are already correctly configured in the file. Once you have updated the placeholders, import the file into BTP:

1. Go to BTP Cockpit → Connectivity → Destinations then click Create.

2. In the Create New Destination dialog box, select From File to import an already configured destination.

3. Select sfsf-conn.properties from your local machine, then click Open.

4. Destination successfully imported, Click OK.

5. On the destination detail page, click Check Connection. A successful Check Connection confirms the destination is correctly configured and reachable.

Principal Propagation from Joule to Agent

With Joule’s Pro-Code Extensibility, customers can seamlessly integrate custom, code-based agents into the Joule ecosystem using third-party frameworks—a paradigm known as "Bring Your Own Agent" (BYOA). Rather than relying solely on declarative Joule frameworks, a BYOA agent operates as a standard, code-based application that communicates directly with Joule via the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol. However, extending Joule’s capabilities with custom logic requires careful consideration of how enterprise data is accessed.

For any production-grade agent interacting with core enterprise platforms like SAP SuccessFactors, implementing Principal Propagation (User Identity Propagation) is non-negotiable. Omitting identity propagation forces the agent to execute requests under a generic technical user identity, which inherently bypasses individual Role-Based Permissions (RBP) and exposes the organization to major architectural, security, and governance risks.

With principal propagation active, data authorization is enforced directly at the backend source system layer in SuccessFactors. This guarantees that unauthorized data payloads are stopped at the source and never exposed to intermediate agent layers or the client application — making identity propagation the core mechanism for maintaining strict enterprise compliance.

Achieving this level of security requires building a continuous chain of trust across the SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP). The previous steps established the connection between SAP SuccessFactors and the BTP environment to enable user-propagated API calls. The next phase establishes trust between Joule and the agent. The resulting end-to-end authentication pipeline flows from the Joule-managed SAP Identity Authentication Service (IAS) tenant, through the agent, and directly into SAP SuccessFactors — yielding a stateless, credential-less agent that holds no long-lived backend credentials, ensuring every backend request is executed strictly within the real-time permissions of the logged-in user.

The setup for establishing trust between Joule and the agent follows the foundation outlined by Felix Bartler in his article, Joule A2A: Propagate the User Identity from Joule into S/4HANA. You may follow the steps directly from Felix's guide or proceed with the tailored implementation steps outlined below.

Registering the IAS Applications for App-to-App Trust

IAS acts as the gatekeeper for every token exchange in this chain. Before Joule can hand its token to your agent, IAS needs to know who each participant is and needs explicit authorization for each step in the exchange. That means registering two OpenID Connect applications — one representing the proxy, one representing your agent — and then drawing the permission path between them.

Both applications must be created in the same IAS tenant where your BTP subaccount established trust during Joule provisioning. You can confirm which tenant that is under Subaccount → Security → Trust Configuration.

Create the IAS Applications

In the IAS admin panel, navigate to Applications & Resources → Applications and create two OpenID Connect applications:

1. A2A_Proxy_App — the intermediary that receives Joule's token and hands it forward. After creating it, expose an API resource on the application (e.g., a2a_proxy_app_api). This API defines the audience (aud) claim that exchanged tokens will carry, which IAS uses to validate that the exchange is directed at the right target.

2. A2A_Custom_Agent_Apps — the application representing your actual agent, the one that will call SuccessFactors. Expose an API resource here as well (e.g., a2a_custom_agent_app_api), for the same reason.

Configure the Trust Chain

Dependencies in IAS define which token exchanges are permitted. In this setup, you need to configure two specific application dependencies: the inbound Joule proxy dependency and the downstream target application dependency.

1. Joule → Proxy: Locate the pre-existing Joule IAS application in your tenant. Add a dependency targeting A2A_Proxy_App  and select its exposed API. Name this dependency exactly joule-to-proxy — this string is hardcoded into Joule's runtime and cannot be changed.

2. Proxy → Agent: Open A2A_Proxy_App and add a dependency targeting  A2A_Custom_Agent_App. Name it proxy-to-target. This name is your choice, but you will need to reference it exactly in the BTP Destination configuration in the next section.

Because the joule-to-proxy dependency is fixed to your proxy app once, adding a future agent requires only a new IAS application and a new proxy-to-<name> dependency on the same proxy — no changes to Joule's configuration.

Finally, generate a client secret on A2A_Proxy_App under Client Authentication → Secrets. The BTP Destination Service will use these credentials to authenticate as the proxy when performing the second token exchange. Save the client ID and secret — you will need them in the next section.

Bring Your Own Agent (BYOA) and Extend Joule Capabilities

To simplify building pro-code custom agents for Joule, we leverage the SAP A2A Agent Toolkit — a skill for Claude Code that scaffolds a complete pro-code agent alongside a Joule capability and Cloud Foundry deployment config in a single command. Supporting both Python and TypeScript, it seamlessly integrates with LangGraph and SAP AI Core / GenAI Hub, handling everything from agent creation to A2A protocol wiring and Joule registration. You can explore the skill page and find the source code in the GitHub repository.

For this SAP SuccessFactors scenario, you can build the agent and Joule capability from scratch using the toolkit—or take the faster path by cloning this ready-to-use reference template from GitHub, which comes with principal propagation pre-configured. With just a few environment updates, your agent and Joule capability will be ready for deployment.

git clone https://github.com/alphageek7443/sfsf-assistant.git
cd sfsf-assistant

The project structure includes exactly what the toolkit generates:

  • app/ — Core agent implementation and business logic.
  • joule-capability/ — Joule capability definitions and A2A wiring.
  • manifest.yml —Cloud Foundry deployment specification.

Before deploying, let's update the environment placeholders and configuration properties to match your target BTP and SuccessFactors landscapes.

Updating the Cloud Foundry Manifest

The repository comes pre-configured with a manifest.yml structure matching the output of the SAP A2A Agent Toolkit. Open manifest.yml and adjust the environment variables and service bindings to align with your landscape:

applications:
  - name: sfsf-assistant
    memory: 512M
    disk_quota: 1G
    instances: 1
    buildpacks:
      - python_buildpack
    command: python -m app
    env:
      MODEL_NAME: gpt-4.1
      AICORE_RESOURCE_GROUP: default
      IAS_ISSUER: https://your-ias-tenant.accounts.ondemand.com
      IAS_AUDIENCE: your-ias-audience-uuid
    services:
      - your-destination-service
    routes:
      - route: your-app.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

Key Configuration Placeholders to Update:

  • MODEL_NAME & AICORE_RESOURCE_GROUP: Set these to match your active model deployment name and resource group in SAP AI Core / GenAI Hub (e.g., gpt-4o, gpt-4.1, etc.). Ensure your AI Core service binding or secret is configured in BTP to grant access to this model.
  • IAS_ISSUER: Your IAS tenant URL (e.g., https://.accounts.ondemand.com). This must match the exact IAS tenant where you registered the trust and applications earlier.
  • IAS_AUDIENCE: The Client ID of the A2A_Custom_Agent_App (not the proxy app). This is a critical link back to your IAS setup: the agent middleware uses this value to cryptographically verify that inbound user tokens exchanged by Joule are intended for this specific agent.
  • services: Replace your-destination-service with the actual name of your SAP BTP Destination Service instance bound to your subaccount.
  • routes: Update your-app.cfapps..hana.ondemand.com to match your BTP Cloud Foundry region and confirm the route host is unique within your organization.

Deploying the Custom Agent

Provision the Destination Service instance (if not already created) and push the application to Cloud Foundry:

# Create the destination service instance
cf create-service destination lite sfsf-assistant-dest

# Deploy the custom agent
cf push

Once deployed, take note of your application’s live route URL—we will use it later when configuring the BTP HTTP destination to the custom agent.

Key Implementation Patterns

Three core components in the agent application work together to pass the user's identity from the inbound A2A request all the way into SAP SuccessFactors. The agent logic itself (agent.py) remains completely decoupled from security tokens, while two supporting layers handle identity capture and downstream token exchange.

1. Inbound Identity Capture (main.py)

A Starlette middleware intercepts inbound A2A requests, extracts the bearer token, and validates it against your IAS tenant before storing it in the request context:

class IASAuthMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next):
        auth = request.headers.get("authorization", "")
        token = auth.removeprefix("Bearer ").strip() if auth.startswith("Bearer ") else None

        if token and (claims := _verify_ias_token(token)):
            set_user_token(token)  # Store token in context for active request thread

        return await call_next(request)

During local development, setting IAS_ISSUER and IAS_AUDIENCE to local placeholders bypasses token signature checks so you can test using mock tokens without modifying code.

2. Downstream Token Exchange (sfsf_client.py)

When tools fetch data from SuccessFactors, sfsf_client.py retrieves the context token and passes it to the SAP BTP Destination Service via the X-user-token header:

def get_sfsf_token_and_url() -> tuple[str, str]:
    creds = _get_dest_service_creds()
    user_token = get_user_token()

    # Get Destination Service access token
    ds_token = httpx.post(
        f"{creds['url']}/oauth/token",
        data={"grant_type": "client_credentials"},
        auth=(creds["clientid"], creds["clientsecret"]),
    ).json()["access_token"]

    # Request SuccessFactors token with user identity attached
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {ds_token}"}
    if user_token:
        headers["X-user-token"] = user_token  # Triggers SAML assertion for end-user

    dest = httpx.get(
        f"{creds['uri']}/destination-configuration/v1/destinations/sfsf-conn",
        headers=headers,
    ).json()

    return dest["authTokens"][0]["value"], dest["destinationConfiguration"]["URL"].rstrip("/")

Why X-user-token matters: Supplying the X-user-token header instructs the Destination Service to generate a user-bound SAML assertion. If omitted, the service falls back to the technical user configured on the destination, bypassing SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP).

Agent Tool Decoupling (agent.py)

Because the middleware and HTTP client manage identity propagation transparently, tools invoke standard OData calls directly:

@tool
def get_contract_renewal_cases(
    employee_id: str | None = None,
    status: str | None = None,
    department: str | None = None,
    faculty: str | None = None,
    top: int = 5,
) -> dict:
    """Fetch contract renewal cases from SuccessFactors.

    Use this tool to look up employment contract renewals, renewal dates, salary
    adjustments, performance grades, approval/review workflow status, and case notes
    for employees. Also covers vendor agreements and internal service transfers.

    Args:
        employee_id: Filter by employee userId (e.g. '103266'). Use userId, not username — resolve via search_employees first if needed.
        status:      Filter by case status (e.g. 'READY_FOR_SS_REVIEW', 'SS_REVIEWED_APPROVED', 'HRP_VALIDATED')
        department:  Filter by department code (e.g. 'ME')
        faculty:     Filter by faculty code (e.g. 'FoE')
        top:         Maximum number of results to return (default 5)
    """
    filters = []
    if employee_id:
        filters.append(f"cust_Employee eq '{employee_id}'")
    if status:
        filters.append(f"cust_status eq '{status}'")
    if department:
        filters.append(f"cust_department eq '{department}'")
    if faculty:
        filters.append(f"cust_faculty eq '{faculty}'")

    params = {
        "$select": (
            "externalCode,externalName,cust_Employee,cust_department,cust_faculty,"
            "cust_designation,cust_currentSalary,cust_newSalary,cust_salaryAdjustment,"
            "cust_performanceGrade,cust_currentEndDate,cust_proposedEndDate,"
            "cust_durationMonths,cust_discussionDate,cust_status,cust_notes,"
            "lastModifiedDateTime,lastModifiedBy,createdDateTime,createdBy"
        ),
        "$orderby": "lastModifiedDateTime desc",
        "$top": str(top),
    }
    if filters:
        params["$filter"] = " and ".join(filters)

    result = sfsf_get("/odata/v2/cust_ContractRenewalCaseV2", params)

    if isinstance(result, dict) and not result.get("error"):
        records = result.get("d", {}).get("results", [])
        if not records:
            return {
                "message": "No contract renewal cases found",
                "filters_applied": {
                    "employee_id": employee_id,
                    "status": status,
                    "department": department,
                    "faculty": faculty,
                },
            }

    return result

Configure and Deploy the Joule Capability

Open joule-capability/capability.sapdas.yaml. The system_aliases block maps a logical name to a BTP destination. The destination name here must exactly match the name of the BTP destination you will create in the next section to point Joule at your agent:

system_aliases:
  SfsfAssistant:
    destination: sfsf-assistant-auth

Leave it as sfsf-assistant-auth unless you plan to use a different destination name—just make sure they match. Next, navigate to the capability directory, authenticate, and deploy the capability to Joule:

Register the Joule Capability

With the agent running, register the capability with Joule:

cd joule-capability
joule deploy -c ./da.sapdas.yaml -n sfsf_assistant_a2a

This compiles and publishes the capability to your Joule tenant. Once the BTP destination is in place, Joule will be able to route user prompts directly to your custom agent.

Configuring the BTP HTTP Destination (Joule -> Custom Agent)

To execute the downstream authentication flow, construct an HTTP destination in your SAP BTP subaccount using the OAuth2JWTBearer authentication type. This destination incorporates specific properties that instruct the SAP BTP Destination Service to execute the token exchange.

Rather than filling in every property manually, download the pre-built destination file below and import it directly into BTP. You only need to update the placeholder values.

Download: (destinations/sfsf-assistant-auth.properties)

Open the file and replace the following placeholders with your own values:

Destination Configuration Parameters

Configure the destination with the following properties:

Name=sfsf-assistant-auth
Type=HTTP
ProxyType=Internet
Authentication=OAuth2JWTBearer
URL=<your-agent-route>
clientId=<A2A_Proxy_App-client-id>
clientSecret=<A2A_Proxy_App-client-secret>
tokenServiceURL=https://<your-ias-tenant>/oauth2/token
tokenServiceURLType=Dedicated
apptoapp=true
tokenService.body.token_format=jwt
tokenService.body.client_id=<A2A_Proxy_App-client-id>
tokenService.body.resource=urn:sap:identity:application:provider:name:proxy-to-target
tokenService.addClientCredentialsInBody=false
x_user_token.jwks_uri=https://<your-ias-tenant>/oauth2/certs

Four placeholders to fill in:

  • <your-agent-route>:  The Cloud Foundry route URL of your deployed custom agent.
  • <A2A_Proxy_App-client-id>: The Client ID generated for A2A_Proxy_App in IAS -- appears in clientId and tokenService.body.client_id
  • <A2A_Proxy_App-client-secret>:  The Client secret generated for A2A_Proxy_App in IAS
  • <your-ias-tenant>:  Your IAS tenant domain -- appears in tokenServiceURL and x_user_token.jwks_uri

Note: The Name property must exactly match the destination referenced in capability.sapdas.yaml (sfsf-assistant-auth). If you customized the destination alias in your capability file, ensure it matches here character-for-character.

Key Architectural Highlights & Considerations

Proxy Client Credentials: The clientId and clientSecret parameters correspond to the IAS proxy application (A2A_Proxy_App), not the custom agent itself. This destination handles the token assertion request sent to the custom agent. Joule automatically manages the initial authentication flow before resolving this destination.

Dependency Mapping (tokenService.body.resource): This property targets the IAS dependency name. The prefix urn:sap:identity:application:provider:name: must be prepended to the exact target application dependency configured in IAS (e.g., proxy-to-target).

User Token Validation (x_user_token.jwks_uri): This parameter points to the JWKS endpoint of your IAS tenant, enabling the SAP BTP Destination Service to cryptographically validate the inbound end-user token before issuing the downstream assertion. Warning: Omitting x_user_token.jwks_uri causes the Destination Service to fail user token validation and silently fall back to a technical service user, breaking end-to-end principal propagation.

App-to-App Mode (apptoapp=true): Explicitly enables App2App authentication mode within the SAP BTP Destination Service.

End-to-End Execution Flow & Testing

To verify that principal propagation and capability routing function correctly across the entire integration, we test the end-to-end flow in Joule using two distinct user personas with contrasting SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP).

For a visual step-by-step walkthrough, you can watch the video demonstration below or review the conversation screenshots in the following subsections.

Multi-Persona Verification Highlights

HR Manager Persona (Tessa Walker): When logged in as HR Manager Tessa Walker, the custom agent leverages full authorized access to sensitive employee compensation and contract data:

Broad Query & Disambiguation: Tessa prompts Joule to show contract renewal cases and requests details for a specific employee. The agent detects multiple active employee records associated with the target employee, prompts for clarification, and asks the user to select the target record.

Detailed Record Retrieval: Upon selecting the specific user record, the propagated user identity passes through the BTP Destination service and returns comprehensive contract renewal details, including Case ID, Department, Designation, Faculty, Current Salary, New Salary, Duration, HRP Validation Status, and Performance Grade.

 

Standard User Persona (Benney Cobb): When executing the exact same conversation flow as a standard employee, principal propagation ensures that security boundaries are strictly maintained:

Directory Resolution vs. Restricted Contracts: Benney initiates the same query for the employee. While Benney's RBP correctly permits basic user directory lookups (successfully resolving the employee's name to the matching user IDs), subsequent calls to the sensitive contract entities fail to return records due to a lack of HR management privileges.

Controlled Output: After specifying the target record, Joule responds cleanly stating that no contract renewal cases were found for the selected user ID. This verifies that security and RBP are enforced at the backend OData layer without requiring custom authorization logic.

 

 

Conclusion

Extending Joule with pro-code custom agents via the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol unlocks powerful, enterprise-grade extensibility patterns on SAP BTP. By leveraging Bring Your Own Agent (BYOA) architectures, development teams can build tailored AI agents using tools like LangGraph while maintaining strict security boundaries.

Integrating the SAP BTP Destination Service with App-to-App (App2App) token exchange and X-user-token propagation guarantees that every AI-driven tool call respects SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP). This ensures end-to-end data security, user context preservation, and full auditability without compromising the developer experience.

References

  • SAP A2A Agent Toolkit
  • SAP A2A Agent Toolkit GitHub Repository
  • Joule A2A: Propagate the User Identity from Joule into S/4HANA

entry.title: Re: wrong tax is calculating in ME21N.
entry.content:
Since both plants have the same Postal Code, Region, and Tax Jurisdiction Code, and the NAVS condition record is successfully found in both cases, the issue does not appear to be in standard tax condition determination or the plant location data.

The next area to investigate is the data being passed from SAP to Vertex and the response being returned by Vertex for each PO item.

I would recommend reviewing:

  1. Whether the two plants belong to different Company Codes or Purchasing Organizations.
  2. Whether different Ship-From or Ship-To information is being sent to Vertex despite the same plant master data.
  3. The MM tax code determination and tax classification of the material/vendor in both scenarios.
  4. The Vertex interface logs (RFC/XML payload) to compare the actual request and response for Plant 100 versus Plant 200.
  5. Whether a user exit, BAdI, or custom enhancement is modifying the tax-relevant fields before the Vertex call.

Since NAVS is finding a valid condition record in both cases, I would focus on comparing the tax communication structure sent to Vertex rather than the pricing procedure itself. A side-by-side comparison of the Vertex request payload for the taxable PO and non-taxable PO should quickly reveal which field differs and is causing Vertex to return different tax results.

Additionally, please confirm whether:

  • The purchase orders use the same tax code.
  • The company code is the same.
  • The goods recipient and plant address data (street/county/city) are identical in ADRC.
  • Tax is missing completely, or only the deductible/non-deductible portion differs.

If the Vertex payloads are identical and Vertex still returns different tax results, then the issue would need to be reviewed jointly with Vertex support using the transaction trace from both purchase orders.

entry.title: Re: Portugal number range PR missing in digital signature...
entry.content:
Based on your description, I believe there may be a misunderstanding between the billing document number range used by Flexible Billing Document Numbering and the number range/series used for Portuguese digital signature compliance.

A few points to verify:

1) Flexible Billing Document Numbering
The routine assigned through enhancement spot SD_BIL_FLEX_NUMBERING determines which billing document number range interval (for example PR or PG) is used at billing creation time.
The standard billing type configuration can still show number range 19. The runtime routine may override the interval assignment depending on your logic.

2) Record Number Ranges for Digital Signature of Billing Documents
This configuration is intended to register the document series used for Portuguese legal reporting and digital signature processes. The value help typically displays the billing document number range intervals that are recognized by the localization framework. Therefore, if PR is not available, it is worth checking whether the interval has been correctly assigned and activated for the relevant billing type and company code/country combination.

3) Custom Routine
As you already observed, the SAP Help documentation for Portugal localization generally does not require a custom numbering routine. A custom routine is usually only needed when you want dynamic determination of billing number ranges beyond standard billing type assignment.

4) What I would test

  • Create a billing document for Portugal and verify the actual billing document number generated.
  • Check whether the document receives numbers from interval PR or from standard interval 19.
  • If the generated billing document still consumes numbers from 19, then the flexible numbering configuration is not being executed as expected.
  • If the generated billing document consumes numbers from PR, then the digital signature configuration may still need to reference the underlying billing type/series rather than the interval itself.

5) Additional verification

Is PR visible and assigned in the configuration activity for billing document number ranges?  Does the SSCUI for Portuguese digital signatures explicitly support customer-created intervals, or only intervals already assigned to billing types?  Have you completed the "Define Billing Document Number Ranges" and "Assign Number Ranges to Billing Types" activities in addition to the flexible numbering configuration?

My suspicion is that the Portuguese digital-signature configuration expects a number range interval that is formally assigned to the billing type, whereas your current setup assigns PR only through the runtime flexible-numbering routine. In that case, the value help would continue to offer the billing type's configured interval (19) rather than PR.

I would be interested to know the result of a test billing document. Does the actual invoice number come from interval 19 or from interval PR? That will immediately identify whether the issue is in the flexible numbering setup or in the Portuguese localization configuration.

Understanding the selected traffic path helps maintain reliable access, improve the user experience, and reduce avoidable connectivity incidents.

Drawing on my SAP Basis and Technical Service Management background, this article focuses on practical routing considerations for SAP-managed private cloud landscapes: connectivity ownership, BGP advertisements, and the interaction between NAT and return traffic. Azure examples illustrate the concepts; implementation details vary by hyperscaler and architecture.

  1. Know the Connectivity Path and Its Owner

Start by identifying how each subsidiary reaches the SAP-managed network.

These services are grouped by function; their routing behavior and capabilities differ. Their use with SAP-managed systems must follow the agreed architecture. SAP’s Secure Cloud Connectivity article provides an introduction to the main patterns. [1]

In a common Azure design, the customer manages the hub and existing ExpressRoute or VPN connectivity, while the SAP-managed network connects as a spoke. AWS documents both customer-owned and SAP-managed Transit Gateway scenarios. Responsibilities therefore depend on the deployed design. [2][3]

For each connection, document the network prefixes, intended primary and backup paths, routing mechanism, and component owners. Not every propagated route uses BGP: AWS VPC attachment routes, for example, propagate into Transit Gateway through internal APIs. [4]

 

  1. BGP: A Backup Path Can Become Preferred

Multiple BGP sessions can support redundancy. The important question is what each session advertises.

Consider this simplified Azure example. Both connections are operational, and both routes are eligible. All addresses below are illustrative and do not represent a customer or SAP landscape.

 

Connection

Advertised customer prefix

Intended role

ExpressRoute

10.20.0.0/16

Primary

Site-to-site VPN

10.20.1.0/24

Backup

For traffic from the SAP environment toward 10.20.1.50, the VPN route is more specific. Azure’s longest-prefix-match selection therefore favors the /24 route. Describing the VPN as “backup” does not override this selection. [5]

This can also affect return traffic: a request may reach SAP through ExpressRoute while its response follows the VPN. Review both directions when diagnosing a failed connection.

A backup VPN with an established tunnel and BGP session can continue advertising routes. A disconnected tunnel is different: routes learned exclusively through its lost BGP session should be withdrawn after failure detection and convergence. They should not remain indefinitely merely because they were previously learned. [6]

Also distinguish these two situations:

  • Overlapping route prefixes: a /24 within a /16 can be an intentional, valid design.
  • Duplicate address allocations: two subsidiaries using the same subnet create an addressing conflict when connected in a shared routing domain.

Using identical subnet masks does not prevent duplicate addressing. Maintain a shared address inventory and control which prefixes each subsidiary may advertise.

  1. NAT: Check the Address Seen by SAP

Source NAT in the customer network can change the address received by the SAP system.

 

Stage

Illustrative address

Original application source

10.20.1.50

Source after customer firewall NAT

172.20.1.50

Destination of SAP’s response

172.20.1.50

The response must have a valid route toward the translated address and reach a device capable of reversing the translation. With stateful NAT, the appropriate session state must be available on that path.

If the translated prefix is unreachable or the response bypasses the NAT device the application may time out even while BGP sessions remain healthy.

Where NAT is unnecessary, a targeted NAT exemption for customer-to-SAP traffic can simplify the path. Before removing translation, confirm that original address ranges do not overlap, return routes exist, and security rules permit the original sources.

Where NAT is required, align the translated prefixes with routing and filtering policies. Azure VPN Gateway provides BGP Route Translation for its own NAT configuration; this does not automatically account for translations performed by a separate customer firewall. [7]

On Azure, inspect effective routes on the VM’s network interface. Check the route state, prefix, source, and next hop; an entry’s presence alone does not prove it is selected for the destination. [5]

SAP KBA 3336611 provides a reference for standard ECS service ports. SAP Note 500235 covers network diagnosis with NIPING. Use these alongside an actual application test, coordinating access and execution with the responsible teams. [8][9]

Conclusion

Reliable SAP connectivity requires consistent address planning, controlled advertisements, and valid return paths. An established BGP session confirms route exchange, not end-to-end application availability.

Before changing the configuration, verify which address SAP sees, which route is selected, and who owns the next component. These checks provide a practical starting point for preventing and resolving connectivity incidents.
